reproduction.text: Lays eggs; the mother coils around them

iucn.long: Listed as Least Concern by Britannica and zoo sources citing the IUCN; one source says it has not been assessed, so treat this with some care.

overview.text: The Reticulated Python is the longest snake in the world: a non-venomous constrictor of the forests and rivers of Southeast Asia. Its name comes from the net-like (reticulated) pattern on its back. It swims very well, which helped it reach many small islands across its range.

identification.text: A long, fairly slender python with a complex, net-like (reticulated) pattern along the back - the feature that gives it its name.

size.label: Typical adults
size.text: Most adults measure a few metres; zoo sources give a range of about 1.5 to 6.5 m, with 3 to 6 m common.

size.label: Largest records
size.text: The longest scientifically verified specimen measured 6.95 m (22.8 ft) and weighed 59 kg. Reports of snakes up to 10 m exist but are not verified, and sources disagree about them.

distribution.label: Native
distribution.text: Southeast Asia, from Bangladesh and Myanmar through Indochina and the Malay Peninsula to Indonesia and the Philippines, and on islands west of New Guinea.

habitat.text: Tropical forest, usually near rivers and other water.

diet.text: Young pythons eat small prey such as rats; as they grow they take larger mammals - up to deer and pigs - and also birds.

reproduction.text: Lays eggs - usually 20 to 50, though clutches of more than 100 have been recorded. The female coils around the eggs to keep them warm. Well-fed females may breed every one to three years.

conservation.text: Still widespread, but large numbers are collected for their skins, for meat and for the pet trade, and big pythons are often killed out of fear.

taxonomy.text: Long called *Python reticulatus*. Genetic studies published in 2014 moved it, with the Timor Python, into a new genus, *Malayopython*.

funfacts.text: It is the world's longest snake - the record verified specimen was nearly 7 m long.
